title: The Syrian and the Three Women of Cairo
summary: A wealthy merchant from Aleppo named Firas arrived in Cairo, boasting loudly in the caravanserais: 'The people of Cairo are simple folk! ...
keywords: the syrian and the three women of cairo
full_text:
A wealthy merchant from Aleppo named Firas arrived in Cairo, boasting loudly in the caravanserais:
'The people of Cairo are simple folk! No Cairene can outwit a Syrian who has traded in the grand souks of Aleppo and Damascus!'

Three clever Cairene sisters, Amina, Safiya, and Maryam, who managed an inherited pottery shop, overheard his boasting and resolved to puncture his vanity.

The next morning, Amina approached Firas in the spice market, asking with a bewildered expression:
'O noble Syrian merchant, canst thou help me? I have a pouch of dried mountain herbs which my grandmother swore can turn common river mud into fragrant incense. Does Aleppo possess such miracles?'
Firas, eager to claim the secret, bought the pouch of ordinary dried mint for ten silver dirhams!

An hour later, Safiya met him near the Nile bridge, weeping:
'Alas! I dropped my copper bracelet into the river! An astrologer told me that if a Syrian merchant of pure heart throws an onion into the current, the river spirits will bring the bracelet to the surface!'
Firas, wanting to prove his purity, bought an expensive onion from a vegetable boat, tossed it with great ceremony into the Nile, and waited on the bank for two hours while local boatmen laughed at his vigil!

Finally, Maryam approached him, holding an ordinary clay jar:
'Kind merchant, this jar holds the captured North Wind, which brings rain to thirsty crops. I cannot open it, lest it blow away my rooftop.'
Firas, determined to possess such a marvel, offered fifty dinars for the sealed jar.
When he broke the wax seal in his lodgings, nothing came out but a faint smell of vinegar!

The next day, Firas found the three sisters sitting together in their pottery shop, smiling warmly.
Amina handed him back his sixty silver dirhams:
'Take back thy money, merchant of Aleppo. We took thy coins not out of greed, but to teach thee a lesson. Never boast that one city is wiser than another, nor judge the intellect of strangers by thy own vanity.'

Firas blushed crimson, took back his silver, and bowed with genuine humility. He spent the rest of his trading season in Cairo conducting business with quiet respect, learning that boasting is the surest bait for clever laughter.
moral: Boasting of superior cunning in a foreign city leads to comedic defeat; modesty is the safest traveler's guide.
